meta.title: Computers You Never Notice
meta.subtitle: Microcontrollers, firmware and real-time behaviour
meta.description: Long explainer on embedded systems: microcontrollers, peripherals, interrupts, RTOS, power and reliability.

blocks.text:
Most computers have no keyboard or screen. They sit inside washing machines, cars, pacemakers and weather instruments, doing one job for years. These are embedded systems.

They are designed under tight limits on cost, memory, power and time, and they are expected never to crash.

blocks.heading: One chip, one job
blocks.text: A **microcontroller** puts a processor, memory and peripherals such as timers, converters and serial ports on a single chip. Firmware reads inputs, makes decisions and drives outputs in an endless loop, often reacting to events through **interrupts** and sleeping in between to save power.

steps.text: **Read.** Pins, converters and serial buses bring in switch states, sensor voltages and messages from other devices.
**Decide.** Firmware filters the inputs, runs control laws or state machines and checks for faults.
**Drive.** Outputs switch loads, generate PWM for motors and LEDs, and send data onward.
**Sleep.** Between events the processor enters a low-power mode and wakes on a timer or an interrupt.

blocks.heading: Real time means on time
blocks.text: In a real-time system a correct answer delivered late is a wrong answer. An airbag controller or a flight controller must respond within a guaranteed deadline. Designers bound the worst-case execution time, give urgent work priority and keep interrupt handlers short. A real-time operating system schedules tasks so those deadlines are met predictably.

items.title: Interrupt
items.text: A hardware signal that pauses normal code to service an urgent event.

items.title: RTOS
items.text: A small operating system that schedules tasks by priority with predictable timing.

items.title: Watchdog timer
items.text: A timer that resets the system if firmware stops responding.

items.title: Bootloader

blocks.heading: Designing for the field
blocks.text: Embedded devices run unattended, often on batteries and in harsh conditions. Engineers must handle brown-outs, electrical noise and corrupted memory, provide safe firmware updates, and increasingly defend against attackers. Connected devices with weak security have become a route into larger networks.

items.title: Vehicles

items.text: Thermostats, washing machines and air conditioners.

items.title: Field instruments
items.text: Data loggers, weather sensors and radiosondes.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of a watchdog timer?
options: Reset the system if the firmware hangs
blocks.explanation: Firmware must 'kick' the watchdog regularly. If it stops, the watchdog forces a reset.

blocks.question: Which statement best describes a hard real-time system?
options: It runs as fast as possible
Missing a deadline counts as a failure
It has more than one processor
blocks.explanation: Timing guarantees, not raw speed, define real-time behaviour.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Firmware**: software stored in a device's non-volatile memory. **PWM**: pulse-width modulation. **ADC/DAC**: analogue-to-digital and digital-to-analogue converters. **ISR**: interrupt service routine. **Bare metal**: firmware running without an operating system.
